t: Followers called themselves Muwahhidun, 'the Monotheists'; the name Wahhabi was probably first used by Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's critic and brother Sulayman, and present-day followers continue to reject it, often calling themselves Salafi.
In 1744 Ibn Abd al-Wahhab formed a pact with the local leader Muhammad ibn Saud, a politico-religious alliance with the Saudi monarchy that lasted for more than 250 years.

Its central teaching holds that devotion to any being other than God, including the veneration of saints at their tombs, is shirk, while its opponents accused it of Kharijite excess and of readiness to declare other Muslims unbelievers.
dyk: Wahhabi scholars of Saudi Arabia allowed paper money in 1951, ended slavery in 1962, accepted the education of girls in 1964 and permitted television in 1965, after vigorous debate.
ev: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab forms a pact with the local leader Muhammad ibn Saud, joining the movement to the Saudi family
Ibn Abd al-Wahhab retires, and the Emirate of Diriyah under Emir Abdulaziz turns to an expansionist policy
The Emirate of Diriyah is destroyed in the Wahhabi Wars
The Ottoman annexation of Al-Hasa leads Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman to write tracts against the Ottomans, Shia and British
Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud and his army conquer Mecca
Saudi Wahhabi religious authorities allow the abolition of slavery
The Saudi clergy expel the scholar al-Albani after a fatwa on women's faces
Saudi Arabia first marks Founding Day on 22 February, dating the state to 1727 and not to the 1744 pact

f.where: Najd in central Arabia, later the wider Arabian Peninsula, Mecca and Medina; Saudi Arabia and Qatar, the two countries whose native population is predominantly Wahhabi, and, through Saudi funding, mosques, schools and scholarships across the Muslim world
f.period: began in the early 18th century; pact with Muhammad ibn Saud 1744; three Saudi States, the first ending with the destruction of Diriyah in 1818; Third Saudi State and Saudi Arabia's oil revenues from 1939; changes to Saudi religious policy from 2017
f.figures: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792), the movement's founder; Muhammad ibn Saud, the local leader of the pact; Hamad ibn Nasir ibn Mu'ammar, who set out its legal theory; Abd al-Rahman ibn Hasan and Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman, heads of the religious estate; Abd al-Aziz ibn Baz and Muhammad ibn al-Uthaymeen, leading scholars of the 20th century
f.outcome: Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's teachings were the official creed of the three Saudi States for more than two centuries; the movement shaped Saudi Arabia's religious institutions and, with Saudi money, spread widely, while its critics call it a deviant sect and its followers reject the name
